note: v:1 means the description was checked against the dish's English Wikipedia article on 13 November 2026. Entries without it are plain translations of menu words.

entries.d: Starters.
First courses: mostly pasta, with soup or rice.
Main courses of meat or fish. They usually come on their own, without sides.
Side dishes, ordered separately.
Desserts.
A cover charge per person. Sometimes written as pane e coperto, bread and cover.
Service charge. Servizio incluso means it is already in the prices.
Of the day, as in piatto del giorno or pesce del giorno.
Of the house: the house wine, or the house speciality.
Off the menu: the day’s specials, often told to you rather than written.
Per 100 grams. Fish sold by weight is often priced this way, so ask how big the fish is.
Frozen. Menus may flag frozen ingredients with an asterisk.
A quarter or half litre: how house wine is ordered by the carafe.
Pasta with grated pecorino romano and black pepper, usually on tonnarelli or spaghetti.
Pasta with guanciale, pecorino romano and black pepper.
Tomato sauce with guanciale, pecorino and chilli. It comes from the town of Amatrice, and in Roman dialect is written matriciana.
Pasta with cured pork, eggs, hard cheese (usually pecorino romano) and black pepper.
Square-cut egg pasta from Lazio, like thick spaghetti. The usual pasta for cacio e pepe.
Thick spaghetti with a hole running through the middle.
Pasta with the intestines of a milk-fed calf. Written pagliata outside Rome.
Gnocchi made from semolina, milk, butter and Parmesan, not potato.
On a Roman menu, a soup: meat broth with shreds of egg stirred in.
Salt-cured pork cheek, the meat in gricia, amatriciana and carbonara.
A hard, salty sheep’s milk cheese, grated over pasta.
Veal with prosciutto and sage, cooked in white wine and butter.
Lamb, cooked the Roman way.
Oxtail stew with vegetables, notably celery.
Beef tripe in tomato sauce.
Offal, literally the fifth quarter: tripe, oxtail, pajata and the like.
Boneless roast pork, fatty and with the skin left on.
Meatballs. Al sugo means in tomato sauce.
Dried, salted cod.
Fillets of salt cod, usually fried.
Chicory shoots, curled in cold water and dressed with anchovy, garlic and vinegar.
Artichokes braised in the pan. A springtime dish in Rome, so in November ask whether they are fresh.
Deep-fried whole artichokes, from Rome’s Jewish cooking.
Chicory greens. Ripassata means tossed in the pan afterwards, usually with garlic and oil.
The pale green, spiky Roman cauliflower.
Courgette flowers.
Roast potatoes.
Mixed salad.
Mushrooms.
Beans.
A fried ball of rice in tomato sauce with mozzarella in the middle. Supplì al telefono is named for the strings of cheese.
Pizza baked in rectangular trays and sold in slices by weight.
Plain pizza bread with oil and salt, eaten on its own or filled.
An oval flatbread sold as a lighter kind of pizza. It is a modern product; the ancient Roman origin story was marketing.
A pocket of pizza bread with a filling, invented in Rome by Stefano Callegari.
A Tuscan flatbread, used for filled sandwiches.
Grilled bread with garlic, olive oil and salt, often topped with tomato.
Fish of the day. Pescato del giorno means the day’s catch.
Sea bass.
Gilthead bream.
Turbot.
Sole.
Amberjack.
Tuna.
Swordfish.
Red mullet.
Anchovies.
Squid.
Cuttlefish.
Octopus. Moscardini are baby octopus.
Prawns.
Langoustines.
Mussels.
Clams.
Oysters.
Raw fish or raw seafood.
Raw fish, chopped or sliced thin.
A mixed fry: small pieces deep-fried in oil.
White fish poached in a light, herbed broth, sometimes with tomato.
Fish soup or stew.
Grilled.
Baked or roasted in the oven.
Fried.
Stewed.
Baked in a paper parcel.
Baked in a crust of salt.
Stuffed.
Smoked.
Spicy.
Without tomato.
In tomato sauce.
A sweet bun split and filled with whipped cream.
The Italian croissant, eaten at breakfast.
A baked tart, often with jam.
Coffee-soaked sponge fingers under a cream of egg yolks, sugar and mascarpone, dusted with cocoa.
Shaved ice with sweet syrup, sold from kiosks.
A bitter herbal liqueur, drunk after the meal.
